title: Explorers or boys messing about?
author: Steven Morris
blurb: A news article about a costly helicopter rescue in Antarctica. Morris uses irony and scepticism to ask whether these men are really explorers.
source: by Steven Morris - Adapted from The Guardian, 28 January 2003
heading: Explorers or boys messing about? Either way, taxpayer gets rescue bill
standfirst: Helicopter duo plucked from liferaft after Antarctic crash

paragraphs.html: Their last expedition ended in farce when the Russians threatened to send in military planes to intercept them as they tried to cross into Siberia via the icebound Bering Strait.
Yesterday a new adventure undertaken by British explorers Steve Brooks and Quentin Smith almost led to tragedy when their helicopter plunged into the sea off Antarctica.

The men were plucked from the icy water by a Chilean naval ship after a nine-hour rescue which began when Mr Brooks contacted his wife, Jo Vestey, on his satellite phone asking for assistance. The rescue involved the Royal Navy, the RAF and British coastguards.
Last night there was resentment in some quarters that the men's adventure had cost the taxpayers of Britain and Chile tens of thousands of pounds.
Experts questioned the wisdom of taking a small helicopter — the four-seater Robinson R44 has a single engine — into such a hostile environment.

There was also confusion about what exactly the men were trying to achieve. A website set up to promote the Bering Strait expedition claims the team were planning to fly from the north to south pole in their "trusty helicopter".
But Ms Vestey claimed she did not know what the pair were up to, describing them as "boys messing about with a helicopter".

The drama began at around 1am British time when Mr Brooks, 42, and 40-year-old Mr Smith, also known as Q, ditched into the sea 100 miles off Antarctica, about 36 miles north of Smith Island, and scrambled into their liferaft.
Mr Brooks called his wife in London on his satellite phone. She said: "He said they were both in the liferaft but were okay and could I call the emergency people?"
Meanwhile, distress signals were being beamed from the ditched helicopter and from Mr Brooks' Breitling emergency watch, a wedding present.
The signals from the aircraft were deciphered by Falmouth coastguard and passed on to the rescue coordination centre at RAF Kinloss in Scotland.
The Royal Navy's ice patrol ship, HMS Endurance, which was 180 miles away surveying uncharted waters, began steaming towards the scene and dispatched its two Lynx helicopters.
One was driven back because of poor visibility but the second was on its way when the men were picked up by a Chilean naval vessel at about 10.20am British time.
Though the pair wore survival suits and the weather at the spot where they ditched was clear, one Antarctic explorer told Mr Brooks' wife it was "nothing short of a miracle" that they had survived.

Both men are experienced adventurers. Mr Brooks, a property developer from London, has taken part in expeditions to 70 countries in 15 years. He has trekked solo to Everest base camp and walked barefoot for three days in the Himalayas. He has negotiated the white water rapids of the Zambezi river by kayak and survived a charge by a silver back gorilla in the Congo. He is also a qualified mechanical engineer and pilot.
He and his wife spent their honeymoon flying the helicopter from Alaska to Chile. The 16,000-mile trip took three months.
Mr Smith, also from London, claims to have been flying since the age of five. He has twice flown a helicopter around the globe and won the world freestyle helicopter flying championship.
Despite their experience, it is not the first time they have hit the headlines for the wrong reasons.

In April, Mr Brooks and another explorer, Graham Stratford, were poised to become the first to complete a crossing of the 56-mile wide frozen Bering Strait between the US and Russia in an amphibious vehicle, Snowbird VI, which could carve its way through ice floes and float in the water in between.
But they were forced to call a halt after the Russian authorities told them they would scramble military helicopters to lift them off the ice if they crossed the border.
Ironically, one of the aims of the expedition, for which Mr Smith provided air back-up, was to demonstrate how good relations between east and west had become.

The wisdom of the team's latest adventure was questioned by, among others, Günter Endres, editor of Jane's Helicopter Markets and Systems, said: "I'm surprised they used the R44. I wouldn't use a helicopter like that to go so far over the sea. It sounds as if they were pushing it to the maximum".
A spokesman for the pair said it was not known what had gone wrong. The flying conditions had been "excellent".
The Ministry of Defence said the taxpayer would pick up the bill, as was normal in rescues in the UK and abroad. The spokesperson said it was "highly unlikely" it would recover any of the money.

Last night the men were on their way to the Chilean naval base Eduardo Frei, where HMS Endurance was to pick them up. Ms Vestey said: "They have been checked and appear to be well. I don't know what will happen to them once they have been picked up by HMS Endurance — they'll probably have their bottoms kicked and be sent home the long way".

opening-hook.what: A farce is a stage comedy where everything goes wrong, and Morris opens with one.
opening-hook.effect: We meet the men as figures of fun before we hear about the crash.

dramatic-threat.quote: threatened to send in military planes
dramatic-threat.what: A whole country's air force was ready to deal with a couple of adventurers.
dramatic-threat.effect: The mismatch is comic, and their last trip sounds like an international row.

icebound.what: 'Icebound' means locked in ice, reminding us how harsh the places they choose are.
icebound.effect: It plants the idea that the men take needless risks.

time-marker.what: 'Yesterday' jumps straight from the old failure to the new one.
time-marker.effect: The crash looks like the next chapter in a run of mishaps.

new-adventure.what: 'Adventure' sounds fun, and 'new' hints at many such trips.
new-adventure.effect: Placed just before the crash, the cheerful word turns sour.

almost-tragedy.what: 'Tragedy' suggests death, so 'almost' shows how close the men came to dying.
almost-tragedy.effect: Their choice to fly there looks reckless because lives were at risk.

dramatic-verb.what: 'Plunged' suggests a sudden, steep fall, where Morris could have chosen 'landed'.
dramatic-verb.effect: We picture a total loss of control, which hardly fits skilled pilots.

rescue-verb.what: 'Plucked', used for fruit or feathers, sits in a passive sentence where the men do nothing.
rescue-verb.effect: The 'explorers' now look small and helpless, saved by others.

icy-water.what: 'Icy' reminds us that nobody survives long in this sea.
icy-water.effect: We feel how real the danger was, for the men and the rescuers.

duration-emphasis.what: 'Nine-hour' counts the cost in time before Morris mentions money.
duration-emphasis.effect: It prepares us for the complaint about taxpayers that follows.

tripling.quote: the Royal Navy, the RAF and British coastguards
tripling.what: Three large public services were needed to save two men.
tripling.effect: The rescue sounds huge for what was a private trip.

resentment.what: 'Resentment' means bitter anger at unfairness, far stronger than 'concern'.
resentment.effect: 'In some quarters' lets Morris report the anger without owning it.

cost-emphasis.quote: the taxpayers of Britain and Chile tens of thousands of pounds
cost-emphasis.what: Morris names who paid and how much, ending the sentence on the money.
cost-emphasis.effect: Taxpaying readers may feel their money was spent on someone else's hobby.

experts.what: Opening with 'Experts' frames everything that follows as informed judgment.
experts.effect: Morris can criticise the men without seeming to attack them himself.

wisdom.what: Questioning someone's 'wisdom' is a polite way to call them foolish.
wisdom.effect: Readers fill in the blunt version themselves: this was a silly plan.

small-helicopter.what: The plain word 'small' sits against a 'hostile environment'.
small-helicopter.effect: The machine looks badly matched to the danger, so we doubt their planning.

single-engine.what: Morris breaks into the sentence to add 'single engine': if it fails, nothing keeps them airborne.
single-engine.effect: The risk was obvious, so the men should have known better.

hostile.what: Personification gives a place human feelings: 'hostile' makes Antarctica sound like an enemy.
hostile.effect: Flying a small helicopter into enemy land looks careless.

confusion.what: 'Confusion' suggests no one could say what the trip was for.
confusion.effect: Without a clear goal, the costly rescue is even harder to justify.

trusty-irony.what: Scare quotes (quotation marks that cast doubt) pick out the team's own boast.
trusty-irony.effect: The 'trusty' helicopter has just crashed, so the boast turns against them.

did-not-know.what: Right after the website's grand claims, his own wife 'did not know' the plan.
did-not-know.effect: The plan seems vague, and the confusion deepens.

boys-messing.quote: boys messing about with a helicopter
boys-messing.what: 'Boys' and 'messing about' suggest children playing with a toy.
boys-messing.effect: The phrase also opens the headline, so his wife's fond joke frames the whole article.

drama-begins.what: 'The drama began' switches from news report to storytelling, like the start of a film.
drama-begins.effect: 'Drama' also hints at a fuss made for attention.

nickname.what: 'Q' is an allusion (a hint) to the gadget expert in the James Bond films.
nickname.effect: The men seem to see themselves as film heroes, which looks silly after a crash.

ditched.what: 'Ditched' is pilots' jargon (specialist language) for an emergency landing on water.
ditched.effect: The accurate term makes the report, and its criticism, seem trustworthy.

distances.quote: 100 miles off Antarctica, about 36 miles north of Smith Island
distances.what: Exact distances pin down how remote the crash was.
distances.effect: The figures sound reliable and show that help was far away.

scrambled.what: 'Scrambled' suggests moving fast and clumsily, on hands and knees.
scrambled.effect: Two men clambering in panic hardly fits experienced explorers.

direct-quote.quote: He said they were both in the liferaft but were okay and could I call the emergency people?
direct-quote.what: 'The emergency people' sounds like a phrase for a minor problem at home.
direct-quote.effect: The calm tone makes a deadly crisis sound ordinary, which is quietly funny.

luxury-detail.quote: Mr Brooks' Breitling emergency watch, a wedding present
luxury-detail.what: Morris did not need the brand, 'Breitling', or the wedding present to report the signal.
luxury-detail.effect: The detail quietly reminds us that these rich men's risks are paid for publicly.

nautical-verb.what: 'Steaming' is a sailing term for a ship moving fast and with purpose.
nautical-verb.effect: The competent navy makes the two men in a liferaft look worse.

miracle-quote.what: Morris first notes the survival suits and clear weather, then calls it a 'miracle'.
miracle-quote.effect: Even with every advantage they needed luck, which says little for their skill.

credentials.what: The men's achievements only appear in paragraph 15, after the farce, crash and anger.
credentials.effect: Our first impression is fixed, so the praise struggles to change it.

class-marker.what: Morris chooses to mention a job that suggests money.
class-marker.effect: A rich man's hobby paid for by the public can feel unfair.

impressive-detail.what: A three-month honeymoon flight shows time and money most readers lack.
impressive-detail.effect: Envy sharpens readers' annoyance at paying for the rescue.

undermining-transition.what: 'Despite' sets all the skills just listed against their record.
undermining-transition.effect: Two words undercut a whole paragraph of praise.

pattern-criticism.quote: it is not the first time they have hit the headlines for the wrong reasons
pattern-criticism.what: 'For the wrong reasons' is understatement: a mild way to say they keep getting into trouble.
pattern-criticism.effect: The crash becomes a habit, which is harder to excuse than one accident.

failure-pattern.quote: they were forced to call a halt
failure-pattern.what: 'Forced' shows the decision to stop was made for them, by the Russians.
failure-pattern.effect: This is the opening 'farce' told in full, so failure frames the article.

ironically.what: Morris names the irony openly: a trip to show good east-west relations ended in Russian threats.
ironically.effect: Saying 'Ironically' in a news report lets Morris's own view show.

expert-criticism.quote: The wisdom of the team's latest adventure was questioned by, among others, Günter Endres, editor of Jane's Helicopter Markets and Systems
expert-criticism.what: A long, specialist job title and 'among others' make the critic sound qualified and not alone.
expert-criticism.effect: Readers trust him, so the case against the men grows.

expert-quote.quote: I wouldn't use a helicopter like that to go so far over the sea. It sounds as if they were pushing it to the maximum
expert-quote.what: The first person 'I wouldn't' is a personal verdict from someone who knows helicopters.
expert-quote.effect: Their choice of aircraft now looks like a basic mistake.

excellent-irony.what: Morris ends the paragraph on 'excellent' and adds no comment.
excellent-irony.effect: If conditions were excellent, readers conclude the fault lay with the men or machine.

taxpayer-bill.quote: The Ministry of Defence said the taxpayer would pick up the bill
taxpayer-bill.what: The Ministry of Defence confirms the headline's claim about who pays.
taxpayer-bill.effect: The complaint about wasted public money can no longer be dismissed as gossip.

highly-unlikely.what: 'Highly unlikely' is a euphemism (a gentle way of saying something harsh) for 'no'.
highly-unlikely.effect: Readers decode it and realise the money is gone for good.

wife-comment.quote: they'll probably have their bottoms kicked and be sent home the long way
wife-comment.what: 'Their bottoms kicked' is how people talk about naughty children.
wife-comment.effect: Echoing the headline's 'boys', it leaves us picturing schoolboys in trouble.

farce.meaning: A situation so silly it is laughable
farce.note: Originally a type of stage comedy where everything goes wrong.
farce.effect: Sets a mocking tone from the first line.

intercept.meaning: To stop someone on their way
intercept.note: To catch or block someone before they reach where they are going.
intercept.effect: Suggests the men were seen as a problem to be stopped.

plunged.note: Used for a fast, uncontrolled drop.

hostile.note: Usually describes an enemy. For a place, it means very hard to survive in.
hostile.effect: Makes Antarctica sound like an enemy.

ditched.meaning: Made an emergency landing on water
ditched.effect: The technical word makes the report sound accurate.

scrambled.note: Often means climbing with hands and feet in a hurry.

dispatched.note: Often used for sending help quickly.
dispatched.effect: Shows the navy acting fast and efficiently.

amphibious.meaning: Able to work on land and in water
amphibious.note: Frogs are amphibians for the same reason: they live in both.
amphibious.effect: Even advanced equipment did not bring success.

floes.effect: Shows how hard the crossing was meant to be.

falmouth.meaning: a coastal town in Cornwall, England

overview.heading: Why Morris wrote this
overview.intro: Morris reports the news, but he also steers our opinion.

points.label: To report the rescue
points.text: "plucked from the icy water" gives the basic facts of what happened and who helped.

points.label: To criticise the cost
points.text: "resentment in some quarters" shows public anger at paying for the rescue.

points.label: To question their judgment
points.text: "boys messing about with a helicopter" shows the men as childish and careless.

overview.heading: Who he is writing for
overview.intro: Morris writes for Guardian readers, many of whom pay tax.

points.label: British taxpayers
points.text: "tens of thousands of pounds" makes the cost feel personal to the people who fund rescues.

points.label: Educated, liberal Guardian readers
points.text: Naming "Jane's Helicopter Markets and Systems" assumes readers respect expert sources.

points.label: Readers wary of privilege
points.text: "a property developer from London" hints at wealth that some readers may resent.

overview.heading: Morris's tone
overview.intro: Morris sounds neutral, but his doubt shows through.

points.label: A sceptical headline
points.text: "Explorers or boys messing about?" asks a question that invites readers to doubt the men.

points.label: Dry sarcasm
points.text: "trusty helicopter" uses quotation marks to mock the men's own boast.

points.label: Understated criticism
points.text: "for the wrong reasons" criticises the men gently, which makes the point sound fair.

overview.heading: Language choices
overview.intro: Morris picks words that quietly make the men look foolish.

points.label: Loaded words
points.text: "farce", "plunged" and "scrambled" make the men seem silly, out of control and panicked.

points.label: Expert opinion
points.text: "I wouldn't use a helicopter like that" lets an expert say what Morris only hints.

points.label: Clashing views
points.text: "nothing short of a miracle" sits beside "boys messing about", showing real danger and silliness together.

overview.heading: How it is organised
overview.intro: The order of the article builds a case against the men.

points.label: Opening with failure
points.text: "ended in farce" means we meet the men as failures before we hear about the crash.

points.label: Cost straight after rescue
points.text: The rescue is followed at once by "tens of thousands of pounds", tying the drama to its price.

points.label: Praise boxed in by failure
points.text: The article moves from crash to achievements to past failure, so blunders surround the praise.

points.label: The wife's punchline
points.text: "they'll probably have their bottoms kicked" ends the article on a joke about naughty boys.
